# Access & Roles

Everything the backend does against Google Cloud — answering a chat turn, running
an evaluation, building a corpus — runs as *you*, under your own Google account.
So what you can do is decided by which role a project admin has granted you, and
the useful question is not "which permissions do I hold" but **"which of the
things I want to do will work."** This chapter answers that, and says how to get
the next role up when it does not.

The roles named here are defined in `deployment/admin/roles.tf` and applied by a
project admin. They are custom roles rather than Google's predefined ones,
because none of the predefined ones can express the distinction the project cares
most about: *create but never delete*.

## What you can do, by role

Each column below is a role you may hold. They **stack** — see
[Roles are layers](#roles-are-layers) — so a maintainer holds `tfaContributor`
*and* `tfaCorpusMaintainer`, and the second column should be read as "what
holding the second role adds."

| What you want to do | `tfaContributor` | `+ tfaCorpusMaintainer` | `+ tfaCorpusAdmin` |
|:---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Run the backend locally and hold a chat turn against the promoted corpus | ✅ | | |
| Run an evaluation with `uv run run-langsmith-evaluation` | ✅ | | |
| Query a datastore directly with `vertex_ai_search search`, to see what retrieval actually returns | ✅ | | |
| Point your `.env` at a candidate corpus somebody built for you, and evaluate it against the promoted one | ✅ | | |
| See which corpus artifacts exist, who owns each, and which leases have lapsed | ✅ | | |
| See which datastores each artifact produced, and which datastores belong to no artifact at all | | ✅ | |
| Build a candidate corpus: upload a document tree, create a datastore, create a search app | | ✅ | |
| Hand a contributor the datastore ID of a candidate you built for them | | ✅ | |
| Promote a candidate, clearing its lease so it stops being disposable | | ✅ | |
| Delete a corpus artifact the reaper will not touch — promoted, unleased, corrupt or orphaned | | | ✅ |
| Restore a bucket that was deleted by mistake | | | ✅ |

: What each role lets you do {#tbl-role-capabilities}

Two things are deliberately absent from every column.

**Nobody holds routine deletion.** Collecting an expired, unreferenced artifact
is the reaper's job, and the reaper is a scheduled service account whose refusal
to delete anything an environment still serves lives in reviewed code in this
repository. `tfaCorpusAdmin` exists for the residue the reaper structurally
cannot reach, not as a faster way to tidy up — see "The roles, and where the
line is drawn" in `deployment/admin/README.md`.

**Nobody holds the ability to grant roles.** That needs
`resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy`, which is the permission that grants
permissions, so it stays with project admins.

::: {.callout-warning title="You authenticate as yourself, never as a service account"}
`mise run //:gcloud-login` writes application default credentials for *your*
Google account, and that is the only credential a person should ever hold here.
The service accounts in this project — the reaper's, CI's — exist to act without
a human, and their keys are long-lived secrets that have to be minted, stored and
later destroyed. If you are ever handed one, something has gone wrong: holding it
is indistinguishable from impersonating the account it belongs to, and the roles
in this chapter stop describing what you can do.
:::

## Roles are layers {#roles-are-layers}

`tfaContributor` is the base that every person holds. `tfaCorpusMaintainer` and
`tfaCorpusAdmin` contain **only what they add on top of it** — neither is usable
on its own. IAM allow policies are additive, so holding two roles gives you the
union, and the grant command binds the whole stack in one go.

The reason is revocation, not tidiness. `tfaCorpusAdmin` is meant to be held for
a task and handed back. If it were a self-contained superset, handing it back
would strip your day-to-day access along with it — and a revoke that breaks
somebody's laptop is a revoke that gets postponed indefinitely. As a layer, it
peels off and leaves you exactly where you were.

::: {.callout-note title="The reaper's role is the exception"}
`tfaReaper` is complete on its own rather than layered. It belongs to a service
account that holds nothing else, and it must not inherit permissions that were
shaped around what a *person* needs — a service account that never looks around
before acting has no business being able to.
:::

## Getting access

Ask in the project Discord, in person, or on a GitHub issue. There is no
self-service path and no form: a project admin runs one command.

```{.bash filename="What the admin runs (from the repo root)"}
# Day-to-day access.
mise run //deployment:grant you@example.com --role contributor

# Someone who will be building corpora.
mise run //deployment:grant you@example.com --role corpus-maintainer

# Break glass, for a task, lapsing after a week.
mise run //deployment:grant you@example.com --role corpus-admin --expires 7
```

`--role corpus-maintainer` binds the whole stack, so there is no need to ask for
`contributor` first. `mise run //deployment:list-access` shows who currently
holds what.

::: {.callout-important title="Break-glass grants expire; base layers do not"}
`--expires` time-bounds **only the top layer**. When a `corpus-admin` grant
lapses you drop back to ordinary contributor or maintainer access, not to
nothing. The same is true of `--revoke`, which removes only the layer you name.
:::

## What to do when something is denied

A missing permission surfaces as a `403`, and the commands in this repository
catch it and print the role you need rather than the raw API error. If you hit
one:

1. **Check you are hitting the right corpus first.** A `403` on a datastore you
   were handed the ID for usually means the ID is wrong or the artifact has been
   collected, not that your role is.
2. **Read what the command printed.** Each one names the permissions it needs and
   the role that contains them.
3. **Ask for the layer, not for more.** The roles are narrow on purpose; the
   answer to "I could not delete it" is almost never "grant me delete."

::: {.callout-tip title="If you are reaching for `tfaCorpusAdmin` regularly, something else is wrong"}
Most manual deletions are evidence of a gap somewhere else — a lease that should
have been stamped at creation, a pairing that should have been recorded in a
manifest, a skip reason the reaper should have handled. The fix usually belongs
in the reaper's predicate rather than in a habit of cleaning up by hand.
:::
